mainTopic: The greatness of rain, and how תורה is learned: worthiness, learning together, and humility
overview: This amud opens by closing the discussion about the thanksgiving blessing for rain: we say both endings. The גמרא then praises rain. רבי אבהו says a day of rain is greater than תחיית המתים, while רב יוסף holds it is only equal, which is why rain is mentioned in that ברכה. רב יהודה compares rain to מתן תורה, and רבא says rain is even greater. The פסוק 'יערף כמטר לקחי' then leads to a lesson: תורה is gentle dew for a worthy תלמיד חכם and harsh rain for an unworthy one. רבי בנאה adds that תורה learned לשמה is a סם חיים, and learned שלא לשמה it is a סם המות. A series of teachings follows. Scholars sharpen each other like iron, תורה learned alone does not last and leads to foolishness, and students sharpen their teachers most of all. Worthy students should be sought out and taught. Finally, תורה is compared to water, wine, and milk, which keep only in plain vessels, so תורה lasts only in a humble person. The story of רבי יהושע בן חנניה and the emperor's daughter illustrates this, and the emperor's objection is answered on the next amud.

steps.title: Say both endings of the rain thanksgiving blessing
steps.stepSummary: The previous discussion about how to end the thanksgiving blessing over rain ends with a compromise: recite both endings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say both of them: 'God of thanksgivings' and 'Abundant thanksgivings.'
steps.whatsHappening: This line closes a discussion on the previous amud about the right ending for the blessing said when rain falls. The answer is to say both versions together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two different endings had been suggested for the thanksgiving blessing over rain. Instead of choosing one, the גמרא rules that we combine them, so both opinions are respected.

keyTerms.meaning: God of thanksgivings, one proposed ending
Abundant thanksgivings, the other proposed ending

steps.whatToRemember: When rain falls, the thanksgiving blessing ends with both phrases: אל ההודאות and רוב ההודאות.
steps.confusionAlert: This line belongs to the discussion that came on the previous amud. It is a closing ruling, not the start of the new section on the greatness of rain.

phrases.english: Let us say them both:
'God of thanksgivings' and 'Abundant thanksgivings.'
phrases.notes: Two different closing phrases for the blessing over rain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion earlier about the wording of the thanksgiving blessing for rain.

steps.title: Rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו says a day of rain is greater than תחיית המתים, because rain benefits both the righteous and the wicked.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: The day of rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead. The resurrection is only for the righteous, but rain is for both the righteous and the wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: A new section begins, praising rain. רבי אבהו says rain is even greater than תחיית המתים, and he gives his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His measure of greatness is how many people benefit. תחיית המתים is only for צדיקים, while rain helps everyone, including רשעים, so rain reaches more people.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a running theme: the גמרא keeps measuring rain against the greatest things we know, here תחיית המתים and next מתן תורה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said:
The day of rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead,
for whereas the resurrection of the dead is for the righteous,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִילּוּ גְּשָׁמִים — בֵּין לַצַּדִּיקִים בֵּין לָרְשָׁעִים.
phrases.english: rain is for both the righteous and the wicked.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: גָּדוֹל יוֹם הַגְּשָׁמִים מִתְּחִיַּית הַמֵּתִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new theme, praise of rain, after the closing ruling about the blessing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain is greater than תחיית המתים because it benefits everyone.

steps.title: רב יוסף disagrees: rain is only equal to resurrection
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבי אבהו disagrees with רב יוסף, who holds that rain is only equal to תחיית המתים. That equality is why rain is mentioned in the ברכה of מחיה המתים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this disagrees with רב יוסף, for רב יוסף said: Because rain is equal to the resurrection of the dead, the Sages placed it in the blessing of the resurrection of the dead.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא comments that רבי אבהו's view argues with רב יוסף. For רב יוסף, rain is equal to תחיית המתים, not greater than it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף explains why משיב הרוח ומוריד הגשם is said in the second ברכה of שמונה עשרה, the ברכה of תחיית המתים: the two are equal in weight. רבי אבהו called rain greater, so the two views differ.

keyTerms.meaning: They established it, meaning the Sages placed it in the prayer

steps.confusionAlert: Both רב יוסף and רבי אבהו think rain is a very great thing. They disagree only about whether it is equal to תחיית המתים (רב יוסף) or greater than it (רבי אבהו).
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains a practical feature of our תפילה: why the mention of rain is placed in the ברכה of מחיה המתים.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Rav Yosef,
for Rav Yosef said:
Since it (rain) is equal to the resurrection of the dead,
they established it in the blessing of the resurrection of the dead.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the previous statement conflicts with another אמורא's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רב יוסף, rain is equal to תחיית המתים, which is why it is mentioned in that ברכה.

steps.title: Rain is as great as the day the תורה was given
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה compares the day of rain to מתן תורה, based on the פסוק that compares תורה (לקח) to rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: The day of rain is as great as the day the Torah was given, as it says, 'My teaching shall drop as the rain.' And 'לקח' means only Torah, as it says, 'For I give you good teaching (לקח); do not forsake My Torah.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה makes a new comparison: a day of rain is as great as the day of מתן תורה. He proves it from two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק compares 'לקחי', my teaching, to rain. The second פסוק shows that the word 'לקח' means תורה. Put together, the תורה is compared to rain, so the two are equal in greatness.

keyTerms.meaning: On which the תורה was given
My teaching shall drop as the rain (דברים לב:ב)
Teaching or doctrine; here it means תורה
And it is nothing other than; used to define a word

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
The day of rain is as great
as the day on which the Torah was given,
as it is said: 'My teaching shall drop as the rain,'
and 'lekach' means nothing other than Torah,
as it is said: 'For I have given you good teaching;
do not forsake My Torah.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: גָּדוֹל יוֹם הַגְּשָׁמִים כְּיוֹם שֶׁנִּיתְּנָה בּוֹ תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another statement praising rain, this time compared to מתן תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A day of rain is equal to the day of מתן תורה.

steps.title: רבא: rain is even greater than מתן תורה
steps.stepSummary: רבא says rain is greater than מתן תורה, because in a comparison the smaller thing is compared to the bigger one, and here תורה is compared to rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Rain is greater than the day the Torah was given, as it says, 'My teaching shall drop as the rain.' Which thing is compared to which? You must say: the smaller is compared to the greater.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא uses the same פסוק but goes further: rain is greater than the day of מתן תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When you describe something by comparing it to something else, you use the more impressive thing as the model. Since the פסוק describes the תורה as being 'like rain', rain is the model, so it must be the greater of the two.

keyTerms.meaning: Which is made dependent on which, meaning which is compared to which
You must say; introduces the obvious answer
The smaller is compared to the greater

steps.confusionAlert: רבא and רב יהודה use the same פסוק. The difference is that רבא reads the comparison as showing rain is greater, while רב יהודה reads it as showing they are equal.

phrases.english: Rava said:
It is greater than the day on which the Torah was given,
as it is said: 'My teaching shall drop as the rain,'
Which is compared to which?
You must say: the lesser is compared to the greater.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: יוֹתֵר מִיּוֹם שֶׁנִּיתְּנָה בּוֹ תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב יהודה, using the same פסוק to reach a stronger conclusion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain is greater than מתן תורה, because the smaller thing is always compared to the greater.

steps.title: Contradiction in the verse: harsh rain or gentle dew?
steps.stepSummary: רבא points out that the same פסוק compares the תורה both to forceful rain and to gentle dew.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא raised a contradiction: It is written, 'My teaching shall drop (יערף) as the rain,' and it is written, 'My word shall flow gently as the dew'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא notices that two parts of the same פסוק seem to clash. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rain, and the word יערף, which can suggest breaking the neck (עורף), sound forceful and harsh. Dew is soft and gentle. So which is the תורה like, harsh or gentle?

keyTerms.meaning: Raised a contradiction; pointed out two sources that seem to clash
It is written... and it is written; the standard way to present two clashing sources
My word shall flow as the dew

phrases.english: Rava raised a contradiction:
It is written: 'My teaching shall drop as the rain,'
phrases.notes: יערף hints at harshness, from עורף, the back of the neck.

phrases.english: and it is written: 'My word shall distill as the dew'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from using this פסוק to praise rain to examining a tension inside the פסוק itself.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two images in דברים לב:ב, rain and dew
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One image is harsh (pounding rain, יערף) and the other is gentle (dew), so the פסוק seems to describe the תורה in two opposite ways.

steps.title: Gentle for the worthy scholar, harsh for the unworthy
steps.stepSummary: The תורה is gentle like dew for a worthy תלמיד חכם, and harsh like rain for an unworthy one.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is a worthy תלמיד חכם, the תורה is like dew. If not, it breaks his neck like the rain.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא resolves the contradiction: each image describes a different kind of person who learns תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two images do not argue with each other; they describe two different situations. For a תלמיד חכם הגון the תורה brings gentle blessing like dew. For an unworthy person it becomes harsh and damaging, 'עורפהו', playing on the word יערף.

keyTerms.meaning: It breaks his neck; a wordplay on יַעֲרֹף

steps.whatToRemember: The same תורה can be gentle dew or harsh rain, depending on whether the person learning it is worthy.

phrases.aramaic: אִם תַּלְמִיד חָכָם הָגוּן הוּא — כַּטַּל,
phrases.english: If he is a worthy Torah scholar, it is like the dew,
and if not, it breaks his neck like the rain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in the previous step.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two cases: each image applies to a different kind of person
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק seemed to describe the תורה in two opposite ways at once.
steps.terutzMaskana: Dew describes the תורה for a worthy scholar; harsh rain describes it for an unworthy one.

steps.title: תורה learned לשמה is a medicine of life
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי בנאה: whoever learns תורה לשמה, the תורה becomes a סם חיים for him. He brings three פסוקים as support.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי בנאה used to say, 'Anyone who learns תורה for its own sake, his תורה becomes a medicine of life for him. As it says: "It is a tree of life to those who hold onto it." And it says: "It will be healing to your body." And it says: "For whoever finds Me finds life."'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that builds on step 7. It shows that the way a person learns decides whether תורה helps him or harms him. This first half covers the good side: learning לשמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 said תורה can be gentle or harsh depending on whether the student is worthy. רבי בנאה names exactly what makes someone worthy: learning לשמה, for the sake of the תורה itself. Three פסוקים from משלי all describe תורה as life and healing for such a person.

keyTerms.meaning: For its own sake, with pure motives

steps.confusionAlert: סַם here does not mean 'poison' on its own. It means a potent substance, like a drug. It can be a סם חיים (life-giving) or a סם המות (deadly), depending on how it is used.

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Bena'a would say:
Anyone who engages in Torah for its own sake —
his Torah becomes for him an elixir of life,
as it is stated: "It is a tree of life to those who hold onto it,"
and it says: "It shall be healing to your navel (body),"
and it says: "For whoever finds Me finds life."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports and explains step 7's idea of a worthy student who receives the gentle side of תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Learning תורה לשמה makes the תורה a life-giving force for the learner.

steps.title: תורה learned שלא לשמה is a deadly poison
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the ברייתא: whoever learns שלא לשמה, the תורה becomes a סם המות for him. This is learned from the word יערף, which means killing.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And anyone who learns תורה not for its own sake, it becomes a deadly poison for him. As it says: "My teaching will drop (יערף) like rain." And עריפה always means killing, as it says: "And they shall break (וערפו) the neck of the calf there in the valley."'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי בנאה gives the bad side: learning שלא לשמה turns תורה into poison. He proves it from the same פסוק about rain (יערף כמטר לקחי) that the גמרא has been discussing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word יערף is matched to the עגלה ערופה, where the calf's neck is broken. That shows the word carries a sense of killing. This fits step 7: the harsh, rain-like side of the פסוק is for the unworthy, and here 'unworthy' means someone who learns שלא לשמה.

keyTerms.meaning: Not for its own sake (e.g., for honor or showing off)
Will drop / will strike (related to עריפה)
The calf whose neck is broken when a murder victim is found and the killer is unknown

steps.whatToRemember: The same תורה can be life or death. Learning לשמה makes it a סם חיים, and learning שלא לשמה makes it a סם המות. This is the 'dew vs. rain' idea from step 7.

phrases.english: And anyone who engages in Torah not for its own sake —
it becomes for him an elixir of death,
as it is stated: "My teaching shall drop (ya'arof) like the rain,"
phrases.notes: דברים לב:ב, the same פסוק discussed in steps 4-7

phrases.english: and arifa means nothing other than killing,
as it is stated: "And they shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא by giving the opposite case to step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Learning תורה שלא לשמה makes the תורה deadly for the learner, as shown by the word יערף meaning killing.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה asks רבי זירא to teach
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks רבי זירא to give a halachic lesson. רבי זירא says he feels too weak, so רבי ירמיה asks for a lighter teaching of אגדתא instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said to רבי זירא: 'Let the master come and teach.' He answered: 'My heart is weak, and I can't.' So רבי ירמיה said: 'Then let the master say something of אגדתא.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short story that sets up the next teaching. רבי זירא can't handle heavy הלכה right now, so he is asked for an easier אגדתא. The next step is that אגדתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is being argued here. The story explains why the next teaching is אגדתא and not הלכה. Learning הלכה takes intense mental effort, while אגדתא was seen as lighter and more refreshing.

keyTerms.meaning: My heart is weak, I feel faint

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה לְרַבִּי זֵירָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said to Rabbi Zeira:
Let the Master come and teach (halakha).
He said to him: My heart is weak
and I am not able.
(Rabbi Yirmeya replied:) Let the Master say a matter of aggada,

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה לְרַבִּי זֵירָא: לֵיתֵי מָר לִיתְנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story that leads into another teaching about תלמידי חכמים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A teaching from רבי זירא, first in הלכה and then in אגדתא.

steps.title: Is a person really a tree of the field?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא quotes רבי יוחנן, who asks about the פסוק 'כי האדם עץ השדה': how can a person be called a tree?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'This is what רבי יוחנן said. What does the פסוק mean when it says, "For man is a tree of the field"? Is a person really a tree of the field?!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא begins the אגדתא. He quotes רבי יוחנן raising a problem with a פסוק that seems to call a person a tree. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, the פסוק seems to say a human is a tree, which makes no sense. The question pushes us to find a deeper meaning for comparing a person to a tree.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of what is written?
And is it so?! (a surprised question)

steps.confusionAlert: In context, the פסוק in דברים כ:יט is really a rhetorical question: 'Is the tree of the field a man, that it should be besieged by you?' רבי יוחנן reads it as a statement, 'man is a tree,' in order to build a דרשה.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן —
phrases.english: He said to him: Thus said Rabbi Yoḥanan —
What is the meaning of that which is written: "For man is a tree of the field"?
And is a man a tree of the field?!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי דִּכְתִיב: ״כִּי הָאָדָם עֵץ הַשָּׂדֶה״, וְכִי אָדָם עֵץ שָׂדֶה הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the אגדתא that רבי זירא gives in answer to רבי ירמיה's request.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain meaning of the פסוק 'כי האדם עץ השדה'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person is obviously not a tree, so the פסוק must mean something deeper.

steps.title: Eat from a worthy scholar and cut off from an unworthy one
steps.stepSummary: Two פסוקים about trees seem to contradict: one says don't cut it down, and one says cut it down. רבי יוחנן explains: a worthy תלמיד חכם is like a tree you eat from and keep, and an unworthy one is like a tree you cut down.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Rather, it is because it is written, "For you may eat from it, but do not cut it down," and it is also written, "It you may destroy and cut down." How do these fit together? If the תלמיד חכם is worthy, "eat from him and do not cut him down." If not, "destroy him and cut him down."'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers his own question. The person-tree comparison teaches how to treat a תלמיד חכם. Learn from a worthy one, and distance yourself from an unworthy one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two tree verses: one forbids cutting down a fruit tree, and one allows cutting down a tree. רבי יוחנן applies them to two kinds of scholars. With a worthy תלמיד חכם, you 'eat his fruit' by learning from him and stay close. With an unworthy one, you 'cut him off' and do not learn from him. This matches the earlier theme that תורה helps the worthy and harms the unworthy.

keyTerms.meaning: How can this be? (introduces how two sources fit together)

steps.whatToRemember: A person is compared to a tree. From a worthy תלמיד חכם you 'eat' (learn) and stay close. From an unworthy one you 'cut yourself off.'
steps.whyThisMatters: This links back to רבי בנאה. A scholar's character and motives decide whether his תורה is something to take in or something to stay away from.

phrases.english: Rather, it is because it is written:
"For you may eat from it, but you shall not cut it down,"
and it is written: "It you may destroy and cut down."
How so?
If he is a worthy Torah scholar —
"from him you may eat, and him you shall not cut down,"
and if not — "him you may destroy and cut down."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 11 by explaining what the person-tree comparison really means.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the verse as a comparison, and splitting two contradicting tree verses between two kinds of scholars.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק literally calls a person a tree, which makes no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tree comparison teaches how to treat תלמידי חכמים: keep and learn from the worthy one, and cut off from the unworthy one.

steps.title: Iron sharpens iron: scholars sharpen each other
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא explains the פסוק 'ברזל בברזל יחד': just as one piece of iron sharpens another, two תלמידי חכמים sharpen each other in הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא said: 'What does the פסוק mean, "Iron sharpens iron"? It tells you that just as one piece of iron sharpens the other, two תלמידי חכמים sharpen each other in הלכה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching about learning תורה. It praises learning together, because two scholars make each other sharper.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When two pieces of iron rub together, both get sharper. In the same way, when two scholars challenge and question each other, both understand הלכה more sharply. This is a new point about the benefit of learning with a partner.

keyTerms.meaning: To tell you (introduces the lesson of a פסוק)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic source for the value of learning בחברותא, with a learning partner.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:
What is the meaning of that which is written: "Iron sharpens iron"?
To tell you: just as with this iron —
one sharpens the other,
so too two Torah scholars —
sharpen one another in halakha.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא, מַאי דִּכְתִיב: ״בַּרְזֶל בְּבַרְזֶל יָחַד״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new series of teachings about how תלמידי חכמים learn תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two תלמידי חכמים learning together sharpen each other in הלכה, like iron sharpening iron.

steps.title: תורה is like fire: it does not burn alone
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה explains that תורה is compared to fire because, like fire, it needs more than one piece to stay alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: Why is Torah compared to fire, as the פסוק says, 'Is not My word like fire, says ה׳'? To teach you: just as fire does not burn on a single stick, Torah does not last with someone learning alone.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching: רבה בר בר חנה gives a reason why the פסוק compares Torah to fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One log by itself does not keep burning, but a pile of wood burns well. In the same way, a person learning by himself does not hold on to his learning or understand it properly. This builds on the previous step, which said that two תלמידי חכמים sharpen each other.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said:
Why are words of Torah compared to fire,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״הֲלֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ נְאֻם ה׳״,
phrases.english: as it says: 'Is not My word like fire, says ה׳'?
To tell you:
Just as fire does not burn on a single piece of wood,

phrases.aramaic: אַף דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֵין מִתְקַיְּימִין בִּיחִידִי.
phrases.english: so too words of Torah do not last with someone alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another teaching on the same theme as step 13: Torah needs learning together.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Torah is not kept properly by someone who learns alone, just as fire does not burn on one stick.

steps.title: Those who learn alone become foolish
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that רבי יוסי בר חנינא said the same idea: there is punishment for those who learn alone, and they become foolish.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: What does the פסוק mean, 'A sword upon the בַּדִּים, and they shall become fools'? A sword upon the 'enemies' of תלמידי חכמים who learn Torah alone (בד בבד). And not only that, but they become foolish, as it says 'and they shall become fools'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports רבה בר בר חנה's idea with a teaching of רבי יוסי בר חנינא about the danger of learning alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word בַּדִּים in the פסוק is read like בַּד בְּבַד, meaning 'one by one, alone'. So the פסוק is read as a warning against learning Torah alone. The word וְנֹאָלוּ adds that such learners become foolish, which matches the idea that Torah does not 'last' when learned alone.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is (what someone else said); a link showing the same idea
the 'enemies' of תלמידי חכמים, a polite way of saying the תלמידי חכמים themselves

steps.confusionAlert: 'Enemies of תלמידי חכמים' does not mean other people who hate them. It is a polite way to avoid saying something bad directly about the תלמידי חכמים. The sword is really on the תלמידי חכמים who learn alone.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא,
phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said,
What is meant by what is written: 'A sword upon the boasters (baddim), and they shall become fools'?

phrases.aramaic: חֶרֶב עַל שׂוֹנְאֵיהֶן שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים
phrases.english: A sword upon the 'enemies' of Torah scholars
phrases.notes: A polite way to refer to the scholars themselves.

phrases.english: who learn Torah alone, each by himself.
And not only that, but they become foolish,
as it says: 'and they shall become fools.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 14 by showing another אמורא said the same idea.
steps.raayaObject: רבה בר בר חנה's idea that Torah is not kept by someone learning alone.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוסי בר חנינא's reading of 'חרב אל הבדים ונאלו' as referring to those who learn בד בבד.

steps.title: Those who learn alone even come to sin
steps.stepSummary: The teaching goes further: those who learn alone also sin, learned by comparing the word ונאלו to a פסוק where it appears together with sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that, but they sin. It is written here 'ונאלו', and it is written there 'that we have acted foolishly (נואלנו) and that we have sinned'.
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching adds a stronger point: learning alone can also lead to sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from the same word in two places. In במדבר, אהרן says 'נואלנו' together with 'חטאנו', so this word is connected to sin. Therefore 'ונאלו' in our פסוק also hints that those who learn alone come to sin, probably because they can reach wrong halachic conclusions without anyone to correct them.

keyTerms.meaning: and it is written there; used to compare two פסוקים

phrases.english: And not only that, but they sin.
It is written here: 'and they shall become fools,'
and it is written there: 'for that we acted foolishly and for that we sinned.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 15, adding sin on top of foolishness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Those who learn alone come to sin, learned from the word ונאלו matching נואלנו next to חטאנו.

steps.title: A second source for the sin: the princes of Egypt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers another פסוק to show that נואלו is linked to sin: the foolish princes of צען led Egypt astray.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say it is learned from here: 'The princes of צען became fools... they led Egypt astray.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different source for the same point that ונאלו means sinning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ישעיה, the word נואלו is followed by 'התעו', 'they led astray'. This shows that this kind of foolishness leads to wrong actions. It is another way to prove the same idea as step 16, not a new idea.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you want, say; introduces another option or source
the princes of צען, a city in Egypt

phrases.english: And if you want, say it is learned from here:
'The princes of Zoan have become fools [etc.]'
'they have led Egypt astray.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different פסוק for the same point made in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word נואלו is tied to leading others astray, so it supports the idea that learning alone leads to sin.

steps.title: תורה is like a tree: a small stick lights a big one
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק explains that Torah is compared to wood because a small stick can light a big one, just as younger students sharpen great scholars.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Why is Torah compared to a tree, as it says 'It is a tree of life to those who hold on to it'? To teach you: just as a small stick lights a large one, small תלמידי חכמים sharpen the great ones.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching from רב נחמן בר יצחק, adding another picture of learning together: small helping big.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 13-14 taught that learning with others is needed. This step adds that even someone smaller, like a student, helps the great scholar. Just as a thin twig is used to start a fire in a big log, a student's questions push the teacher to think deeper.

keyTerms.meaning: to those who hold on to it

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
Why are words of Torah compared to a tree,
as it says: 'It is a tree of life to those who hold on to it'?
To tell you:

phrases.aramaic: מָה עֵץ קָטָן מַדְלִיק אֶת הַגָּדוֹל,
phrases.english: Just as a small piece of wood lights the large one,

phrases.aramaic: אַף תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים קְטַנִּים מְחַדְּדִים אֶת הַגְּדוֹלִים.
phrases.english: so too small Torah scholars sharpen the great ones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern as step 14 (לָמָּה נִמְשְׁלוּ), now with a tree instead of fire, adding that even younger scholars help the great ones.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Younger, smaller scholars sharpen the greater scholars, like a small stick lights a big log.

steps.title: רבי חנינא learned the most from his students
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports רב נחמן בר יצחק with רבי חנינא's statement that he learned more from his students than from anyone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבי חנינא said: I learned a lot from my teachers, and from my friends more than from my teachers, and from my students more than from all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבי חנינא's personal experience matches the idea that small scholars sharpen great ones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא ranks three groups: teachers, friends, and students. Surprisingly, students taught him the most, because their questions forced him to explain and think more deeply. This is exactly the 'small stick lights the big one' idea from step 18.
steps.whatToRemember: תורה is best learned together. Like fire, it needs more than one piece, and like wood, even a small piece can light a big one. Learning alone leads to foolishness and even sin. Students, friends, and teachers all sharpen each other, and students do so most of all.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a famous source for the value of חברותא learning and for teaching others as a way to grow in one's own learning.

phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Chanina said:
I learned much from my teachers,
and from my friends more than from my teachers,
and from my students more than from all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 18 with a real-life statement from רבי חנינא.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן בר יצחק's idea that small scholars sharpen great ones.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חנינא's statement that he learned the most from his students.

steps.title: Two verses about thirst and water seem to contradict
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר פפא points out two פסוקים that seem to disagree. One says to bring water to the thirsty person. The other says the thirsty person must go to the water himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר פפא raised a contradiction. One פסוק says: 'Bring water toward the thirsty one.' Another פסוק says: 'Ho, everyone who is thirsty, go to the water.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a contradiction between two פסוקים about water, which stands for Torah. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first פסוק, the one who has the water goes to the thirsty person. In the second, the thirsty person must go to the water. Since water means Torah, the question is who should go to whom: the teacher to the student, or the student to the teacher?

keyTerms.meaning: He raised a contradiction (literally 'he threw' two sources against each other)
Thirsty person (here, someone who wants to learn Torah)

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa raised a contradiction:
It is written: "Toward the thirsty one, bring water"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו כא:יד. The water comes to the thirsty person.

phrases.english: And it is written: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, go to the water."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו נה:א. The thirsty person must go to the water.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the teacher-student theme from steps 18-19 with a new contradiction between פסוקים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two פסוקים in ישעיהו about water and the thirsty
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק says the water comes to the thirsty person, and the other says the thirsty person goes to the water. These directions seem to clash.

steps.title: Worthy students are sought out; others must seek
steps.stepSummary: Resolution: if the student is worthy, the teacher goes to him. If not, the student must go to find Torah himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is a worthy student, then 'bring water toward the thirsty one.' If not, then 'everyone who is thirsty, go to the water.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא בר פפא resolves his own contradiction by saying the two פסוקים describe two different kinds of students.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוקים do not argue. Each one applies to a different case. A worthy student deserves to have the teacher come to him. An unworthy student must make the effort and go to a teacher.

phrases.english: If he is a worthy student,
"Toward the thirsty one, bring water"
and if not,
"Ho, everyone who thirsts, go to the water."
phrases.notes: The student must go to the teacher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting cases (each פסוק refers to a different type of student)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוקים seem to give opposite rules about who goes to whom.
steps.terutzMaskana: A worthy student is sought out by the teacher. An unworthy student must seek out the teacher himself.

steps.title: Share your springs, or keep them to yourself?
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר חמא points out two neighboring פסוקים in משלי. One says to spread your springs outside. The next says to keep them for yourself alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר חמא raised a contradiction. One פסוק says: 'Let your springs spread outside.' The next says: 'Let them be for you alone.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second contradiction between פסוקים, also about sharing Torah. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The springs stand for a teacher's Torah. One פסוק says to share it widely. The very next פסוק says to keep it private, so the question is whether a teacher should share his Torah.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Ḥama raised a contradiction:
It is written: "Let your springs spread outside"
And it is written: "Let them be for you alone."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel contradiction to step 20, again about teaching students.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק says to share your springs outside, and the next says to keep them only for yourself. These seem opposite.

steps.title: Teach a worthy student; keep תורה from an unworthy one
steps.stepSummary: Resolution: with a worthy student, spread your Torah. With an unworthy student, keep it to yourself.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is a worthy student, then 'let your springs spread outside.' If not, then 'let them be for you alone.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא בר חמא settles the contradiction the same way as before: it depends on whether the student is worthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A teacher should share his Torah with a fitting student. He should not teach it to someone unworthy. Both פסוקים are true, each in its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: And if not (Hebrew form of וְאִי לָא)

steps.whatToRemember: Two contradictions, one answer. Whether a teacher seeks out a student, and whether he shares his Torah with him, depends on whether the student is a תלמיד הגון.

phrases.english: If he is a worthy student,
"Let your springs spread outside"
and if not,
"Let them be for you alone."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction in step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting cases (worthy student vs. unworthy student)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוקים seem to say both 'share' and 'do not share.'
steps.terutzMaskana: Share Torah with a worthy student. Keep it from an unworthy one.

steps.title: תורה is like water: it flows to the humble
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר אידי explains why Torah is compared to water. Water leaves high places and flows down to low places, and Torah likewise stays only with a humble person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר אידי said: Why is Torah compared to water, as it says, 'Ho, everyone who thirsts, go to the water'? To teach you: just as water leaves a high place and flows to a low place, so Torah lasts only in someone whose mind is humble.
steps.whatsHappening: Using the water פסוק just quoted, a new teaching explains what the comparison of Torah to water means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water does not stay on a mountaintop. It runs down to the lowest point. In the same way, Torah does not stay with a proud person. It settles in someone who thinks of himself as low.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose mind is lowly, meaning humble

phrases.english: And Rabbi Ḥanina bar Idi said:
Why are words of Torah compared to water,
as it is written: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, go to the water"?
To tell you:
just as water leaves a high place
and goes to a low place,
so too, words of Torah last
only in one whose mind is humble.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the water פסוק from steps 20-21 and asks what the water comparison teaches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Torah lasts only in a humble person, just as water flows only to low places.

steps.title: Water, wine, and milk keep best in plain vessels
steps.stepSummary: רבי אושעיא explains why Torah is compared to water, wine, and milk. These drinks keep only in simple, cheap vessels, and Torah likewise lasts only in a humble person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אושעיא said: Why is Torah compared to these three drinks, water, wine, and milk? The פסוק says 'go to the water' and 'go buy wine and milk without money.' To teach you: just as these drinks keep only in the plainest vessels, so Torah lasts only in a humble person.
steps.whatsHappening: A second teaching adds to the previous one with a different comparison, this time using three drinks instead of just water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water, wine, and milk spoil in fancy gold or silver vessels and keep best in simple clay ones. A person who sees himself as simple and plain is the kind of 'vessel' where Torah stays. This reaches the same conclusion as רבי חנינא בר אידי through a new image.

keyTerms.meaning: The lowliest, cheapest of vessels (like clay pots)

steps.whatToRemember: Both comparisons, water flowing downhill and drinks kept in plain vessels, teach one lesson: תורה lasts only in someone who is humble.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Oshaya said:
Why are words of Torah compared
to these three drinks:
to water, to wine, and to milk?
As it is written: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, go to the water,"
and it is written: "Go, buy and eat,
and go buy, without money
and without price, wine and milk."
To tell you:

phrases.aramaic: מָה שְׁלֹשָׁה מַשְׁקִין הַלָּלוּ אֵין מִתְקַיְּימִין
phrases.english: just as these three drinks keep
only in the lowliest of vessels,
phrases.notes: Such as clay pots. In gold or silver vessels they spoil.

phrases.english: so too, words of Torah last
only in one whose mind is humble.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels step 24, reaching the same lesson of humility through a three-drink comparison.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Torah lasts only in a humble person, just as water, wine, and milk keep only in the plainest vessels.

steps.title: The emperor's daughter mocks a wise but ugly sage
steps.stepSummary: The emperor's daughter says it is a shame that great wisdom sits in an ugly body. רבי יהושע בן חנניה answers by asking what kind of jars her father keeps his wine in.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what the emperor's daughter said to רבי יהושע בן חנניה: 'What a pity, such glorious wisdom in such an ugly vessel!' He said to her: 'Does your father keep his wine in clay jars?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story to illustrate רבי אושעיא's teaching that Torah only lasts in a humble, plain 'vessel.' The sage's odd question about wine is setting up his lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The princess calls רבי יהושע's body an ugly 'vessel' for his wisdom. He does not argue with her. Instead he switches to wine jars, which is the exact image רבי אושעיא used, so he can teach her through her own household.

keyTerms.meaning: An ugly vessel (here: an ugly body)

phrases.english: As the emperor's daughter said
to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya:
phrases.notes: He was known to be very unattractive.

phrases.english: Woe to glorious wisdom in an ugly vessel!
He said to her: Does your father put wine
in clay vessels?

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדַאֲמַרָה לֵיהּ בְּרַתֵּיה דְּקֵיסָר לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story that illustrates רבי אושעיא's teaching about cheap vessels.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story begins: a wise man in an ugly body answers mockery with a question about wine jars.

steps.title: The sage tells her to use gold and silver vessels
steps.stepSummary: The princess asks what else her father should use. רבי יהושע בן חנניה says that important people like them should use gold and silver.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said to him: 'Then what should he keep it in?' He said to her: 'You, who are so important, should put it in vessels of gold and silver.'
steps.whatsHappening: The princess takes the bait and asks what to use instead. The sage gives advice he knows will fail, which sets up the test in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The princess assumes clay is the only sensible choice for wine. That is exactly the point: even she knows wine belongs in plain jars. The sage's gold-and-silver suggestion is a planned demonstration, not real advice.

keyTerms.meaning: In what should we put it?

phrases.english: She said to him: Rather, in what should we put it?
He said to her: You, who are so important,
put it in vessels of gold and silver.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the conversation and sets up the experiment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sage suggests fancy vessels in order to prove they are unsuitable.

steps.title: The wine spoils and the emperor summons the sage
steps.stepSummary: The wine is moved into gold and silver vessels and turns sour. The emperor learns that רבי יהושע בן חנניה gave the advice and calls him in to ask why.
steps.simpleTranslation: She went and told her father. He put the wine in gold and silver vessels, and it turned sour. His servants came and told him. He asked his daughter, 'Who told you to do this?' She said, 'רבי יהושע בן חנניה.' They summoned him. The emperor said to him, 'Why did you tell her this?'
steps.whatsHappening: The experiment plays out: the wine in the fancy vessels spoils. The emperor demands an explanation, which sets up the sage's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the proof in real life. The plain clay jars kept the wine good, and the expensive vessels ruined it. This matches רבי אושעיא's claim that wine and Torah keep only in simple vessels.

phrases.english: She went and told her father
He put the wine in vessels of gold and silver,
and it turned sour.
They came and told him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לַהּ לִבְרַתֵּיהּ: מַאן אֲמַר לָךְ הָכִי?
phrases.english: He said to his daughter: Who told you this?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה.
phrases.english: She said to him: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya.
They summoned him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַמַּאי אֲמַרְתְּ לַהּ הָכִי?
phrases.english: He said to him: Why did you tell her this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the result of the sage's advice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wine stored in gold and silver vessels spoils.

steps.title: The sage explains his lesson
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן חנניה explains that he was answering the princess's insult. Fine things keep best in plain vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'Just as she said to me, so I said to her.'
steps.whatsHappening: The sage reveals the point of the whole exercise. His advice was a reply to her remark about his ugly 'vessel.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: She mocked wisdom in an ugly body. He showed her that precious things, like wine, actually last better in plain containers. In the same way, Torah lasts in a humble, unimpressive person, which is רבי אושעיא's point.

keyTerms.meaning: Just as she said to me

steps.whatToRemember: The story proves רבי אושעיא's teaching. Wine spoils in gold but keeps in clay. תורה likewise stays with the humble, not with the proud or impressive.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כִּי הֵיכִי דַּאֲמַרָה לִי,
phrases.english: He said to him: Just as she said to me,
so I said to her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כִּי הֵיכִי דַּאֲמַרָה לִי, אֲמַרִי לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the emperor's question and states the moral.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Precious wisdom, like wine, is best kept in a plain vessel.

steps.title: The emperor objects that some handsome people are learned
steps.stepSummary: The emperor challenges the lesson. There are good-looking people who are also learned.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there are handsome people who are learned!
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor pushes back on the sage's lesson. The sage's reply comes at the start of the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If Torah only lasts in a plain vessel, how can there be handsome scholars? The emperor's real-life examples seem to disprove the rule.

phrases.english: But there are handsome people who are learned!
